title: KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step. We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

Post-training quantization (PTQ) to 4-bit precision is the natural way to deploy billion-parameter diffusion transformers (DiTs), and is supported natively in current accelerators via the OCP Microscaling standard (Microsoft et al. , 2023 ) . The bottleneck is activation outliers (Xiao et al. , 2023 ) : a small subset of channels carries magnitudes orders of magnitude larger than the rest, so a 4 4 -bit blockwise quantizer wastes most of its dynamic range on those channels and clips everything else. Consider a linear layer O = A ​ W ⊤ O=AW^{\top} with A ∈ ℝ m × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} , W ∈ ℝ o × d W\in\mathbb{R}^{o\times d} , and a b b -bit quantizer Q b Q_{b} . The main solution in both LLM and DiT quantizers is to insert an invertible activation transform T ∈ GL ​ ( d ) T\in\mathrm{GL}(d) that redistributes channel magnitudes before quantization, acting as A ↦ A ​ T , W ↦ W ​ T − T , A ​ T ⋅ ( W ​ T − ⊤ ) ⊤ = A ​ T ⋅ T − 1 ​ W ⊤ = A ​ W ⊤ , A\mapsto AT,\qquad W\mapsto WT^{-T},\qquad AT\cdot(WT^{-\top})^{\top}=AT\cdot T^{-1}W^{\top}=AW^{\top}, (1) which leaves the linear map invariant while reducing the per-layer quantization error ℰ ​ ( T ) = Q b ​ ( A ​ T ) ​ Q b ​ ( W ​ T − ⊤ ) ⊤ − A ​ W ⊤ . \mathcal{E}(T)=Q_{b}(AT)\,Q_{b}(WT^{-\top})^{\top}-AW^{\top}. (2) The compensating T − 1 T^{-1} is always folded into the layer’s stored weights; the absorption trick further folds T T into the previous layer’s output, so that the activation arriving at the current layer is already T T -transformed and the runtime transform is free. As such, existing methods differ only in the structure of T T : diagonal per-channel scaling (Xiao et al. , 2023 ; Zhao et al. , 2025 ; Wu et al. , 2024 ) , dense rotations (Ashkboos et al. , 2025 ; Tseng et al. , 2024 ; Liu et al. , 2025 ) , or general invertible matrices (Sun et al. , 2024 ) . While generally applicable to LLMs, the absorption trick fails in DiTs, especially between transformer blocks. This is because folding T T into the previous layer’s output requires the normalization between blocks to commute with T T : Norm ​ ( x ​ T ) ​ T − 1 = Norm ​ ( x ) . \mathrm{Norm}(xT)\,T^{-1}=\mathrm{Norm}(x). (3) This is not satisfied by the AdaLN variant sitting between every DiT block (Appendix C ). Every transform a DiT quantizer applies therefore runs online , at every linear layer of every denoising step, and per-step cost becomes the binding design constraint. While the per-step cost is affordable with per-channel scaling transforms that entail diagonal matrices, this strategy offers only limited expressivity and thus quantization accuracy. This trade-off is taken by recent weight-splitting PTQ pipelines such as SVDQuant (Li et al. , 2025 ) and LoRaQ (Bouquet et al. , 2026 ) , which decompose each weight into a low-bit residual and a low-rank correction branch. By contrast, existing non-diagonal transforms yield better quantization but fall short under the online constraint. A Hadamard transform is a fixed orthogonal and symmetric matrix with normalized ± 1 \pm 1 entries that mixes channels via add/subtract butterflies, spreading outlier magnitudes uniformly across the block (Ashkboos et al. , 2025 ) . At block size 32, it is cheap (a single MXFP4-aligned kernel pass) but suppresses outliers only within each 32-channel sub-vector, and eventually ends up underperforming per-channel scaling (Xiao et al. , 2023 ) . Learned d × d d\times d invertible matrices (Liu et al. , 2025 ; Sun et al. , 2024 ) are expressive but store O ​ ( d 2 ) O(d^{2}) parameters per layer and require a dense m × d × d m\times d\times d matrix multiplication every step, infeasible at inference. Altogether, there is therefore a need for a transform that is learned and 32 × 32 32\times 32 block-diagonal ; that is, more expressive than a fixed Hadamard at the same block size, yet online-cheap and compatible with an MX quantizer. To address this need, we propose KroQuant , a learned T T that is block-diagonal with 32 × 32 32\times 32 blocks and a compact parametrization that uses fewer scalars per layer than per-channel scaling, contains the Hadamard as a special case used as initialization, and applies as a single 32 × 32 32\times 32 tensor-core GEMM per block at inference; the construction is detailed in Section 3.2 . We show that KroQuant acts as a drop-in replacement for SmoothQuant (Xiao et al. , 2023 ) in the activation-transform stage of weight-splitting PTQ pipelines such as LoRaQ (Figure 1 ). On PixArt- Σ \Sigma (Chen et al. , 2024a ) , SANA (Xie et al. , 2025 ) , and FLUX.1-schnell (Black-Forest-Labs, 2024 ) , LoRaQ-with-KroQuant matches or beats LoRaQ-with-SmoothQuant (Bouquet et al. , 2026 ; Xiao et al. , 2023 ) and the SVDQuant reference (Li et al. , 2025 ) at W4A4, while the KroQuant quantizer kernel runs up to 14 % 14\% faster than the SmoothQuant kernel on an MI350 GPU. Concretely, we contribute: • A learned block-diagonal activation transform compatible with online constraints. The first non-diagonal online transform for DiT PTQ that is more expressive than a fixed block-Hadamard and cheaper at inference than full- d d rotations (Liu et al. , 2025 ) or invertibles (Sun et al. , 2024 ) . • A Kronecker-LU parametrization of GL ​ ( 32 ) \mathrm{GL}(32) blocks. Five 2 × 2 2\times 2 unit-determinant LU factors yield a stable, 68 × 68\times smaller parameter footprint than dense GL ​ ( 32 ) \mathrm{GL}(32) blocks, with the Hadamard as a natural initialization. • A fused W4A4 kernel. Each block applies as a single tensor-core GEMM; on MI350 the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to 14 % 14\% faster than the SmoothQuant baseline kernel. 2 Related Work PTQ for diffusion transformers. DiT quantization has progressed from 8-bit schemes (Shang et al. , 2023 ) to sub-8-bit methods that adapt SmoothQuant (Xiao et al. , 2023 ) to the timestep-conditioned activation distributions induced by AdaLN. PTQ4DiT (Wu et al. , 2024 ) and ViDiT-Q (Zhao et al. , 2025 ) apply per-channel diagonal scales with timestep-dependent calibration; Q-DiT (Chen et al. , 2024b ) and MixDQ (Zhao et al. , 2024 ) push further with mixed-precision and sensitivity-driven allocations. All keep the activation transform T T diagonal, and all degrade at W4A4, where the residual error is dominated by inter-channel correlations that no per-channel rescaling can remove. The design space of activation transforms. PTQ methods that go beyond per-channel scaling differ in the sparsity pattern of the invertible transform T ∈ GL ​ ( d ) T\in\mathrm{GL}(d) . SmoothQuant’s diagonal T T rescales channels independently; QuaRot (Ashkboos et al. , 2025 ) and QuIP# (Tseng et al. , 2024 ) use fixed dense Hadamard rotations, whose outlier-suppression strength grows with block size but whose full- d d butterfly does not map onto tensor cores; SpinQuant (Liu et al. , 2025 ) and FlatQuant (Sun et al. , 2024 ) learn a dense T T on the Stiefel manifold or in GL ​ ( d ) \mathrm{GL}(d) respectively, at the cost of a d × d d\times d parameter matrix and a dense GEMM per layer. In LLMs all of these absorb offline into adjacent weights through RMSNorm; in DiTs they cannot, as discussed in Section 1 , so per-step cost becomes load-bearing. KroQuant sits between SmoothQuant and FlatQuant: T T is block-diagonal with 32 × 32 32\times 32 blocks, each more expressive than a fixed Hadamard at the same block size, and applied online as parallel tensor-core GEMMs with fewer parameters per layer than SmoothQuant’s diagonal scales. Low-rank weight splitting and the role of the activation transform. A complementary line of work splits the linear-layer weight W W into a low-rank branch and a 4-bit residual. SVDQuant (Li et al. , 2025 ) smooths outliers and SVD-decomposes the smoothed weight with data-dependent low-rank calibration; LoRaQ (Bouquet et al. , 2026 ) instead fits the low-rank branch data-free to the residual quantization error, allowing the low-rank branch itself to be quantized below 16 bits. Both methods split the weight but quantize the activation as-is, so they require an online activation transform with no normalization to fuse against, and both default to a SmoothQuant-style diagonal T T . KroQuant is a drop-in replacement for that transform: we adopt LoRaQ’s weight correction unchanged and substitute its SmoothQuant front-end with our learned block-diagonal T T , yielding the headline LoRaQ-with-KroQuant comparison against LoRaQ-with-SmoothQuant, with SVDQuant as an additional reference. 3 Method We work within the formal setup of Section 1 and instantiate the blockwise quantizer Q b Q_{b} left abstract there as follows. 3.1 Quantization setup We denote by Q b Q_{b} (Section 1 ) the blockwise quantize-then-dequantize operator at bit width b b , taking a real matrix and returning a matrix of the same shape: each row of the input is partitioned into non-overlapping blocks of size n n ; each block is encoded as a shared scale s s (the set of representable scales, e.g., FP8) and a n n vector 𝐪 \mathbf{q} in the chosen b b -bit format (FP4 when b = 4 b=4 ); the dequantized blocks are reassembled into the output. Goal. We want to construct a transform T ∈ GL ​ ( d ) T\in\mathrm{GL}(d) that is block-diagonal, T = diag ​ ( K ( 1 ) , K ( 2 ) , … , K ( ⌈ d / n ⌉ ) ) , T=\mathrm{diag}(K^{(1)},K^{(2)},\ldots,K^{(\lceil d/n\rceil)}), (4) where each diagonal block K ( j ) ∈ GL ​ ( 32 ) K^{(j)}\in\mathrm{GL}(32) , learnable (unlike a fixed Hadamard), and whose parametrization is less than half the size of per-channel scaling and more than 68 × 68\times smaller than a dense GL ​ ( 32 ) \mathrm{GL}(32) block. We aim to leave the linear map invariant ( A ​ T ⋅ ( W ​ T − 1 ) ⊤ = A ​ W ⊤ AT\cdot(WT^{-1})^{\top}=AW^{\top} ) while reducing ‖ ℰ ‖ F \|\mathcal{E}\|_{F} . 3.2 Kronecker-structured invertible block transforms This structure of T T couples features within each group of n n channels while leaving groups independent, matching the block structure of the MXFP4e2 quantizer Q 4 Q_{4} . Kronecker product construction. We parametrize each n × n n\times n block as a Kronecker product of log 2 ⁡ n \log_{2}n small matrices: K n = G 1 ⊗ G 2 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ G log 2 ⁡ n , G k ∈ ℝ 2 × 2 , k = 1 , … , log 2 ⁡ n . K_{n}=G_{1}\otimes G_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes G_{\log_{2}n},\qquad G_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2},\;k=1,\ldots,\log_{2}n. (5) For n = 32 n=32 this gives log 2 ⁡ 32 = 5 \log_{2}32=5 factors. Since the Kronecker product of invertible matrices is invertible, and since ( G 1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ G 5 ) − 1 = G 1 − 1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ G 5 − 1 (G_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes G_{5})^{-1}=G_{1}^{-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes G_{5}^{-1} , inversion reduces to five independent 2 × 2 2\times 2 inversions. The normalized Hadamard matrix H n H_{n} ( n = 2 k n=2^{k} ) is a Kronecker product of k k copies of the 2 × 2 2\times 2 factor 1 2 ​ ( 1 1 1 − 1 ) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 1&-1\end{pmatrix} . This is known empirically as a good initialization strategy to reduce activation outliers and lower quantization error before any gradient-based optimization (Ashkboos et al. , 2025 ; Liu et al. , 2025 ) . 3.3 Layer-wise transform optimization Objective. Given a small calibration dataset providing N N activation samples { A ( s ) } s = 1 N \{A^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^{N} , we optimize T T independently for each linear layer by minimizing the output mean squared error: ℒ out ​ ( T ) = 1 N ​ m ​ o ​ ‖ Q b ​ ( A ​ T ) ​ Q b ​ ( W ​ T − T ) ⊤ − A ​ W ⊤ ‖ F 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\text{out}}(T)=\frac{1}{Nmo}\left\|Q_{b}(AT)\,Q_{b}(WT^{-T})^{\top}-AW^{\top}\right\|_{F}^{2}. (7) Regularization. Minimizing ℒ out \mathcal{L}_{\text{out}} alone can converge to solutions where one operand is well-quantized at the expense of the other — for example, a transform that whitens the activations perfectly while leaving the weights in a highly non-uniform representation. To encourage both operands to be individually well-quantized, we add two auxiliary terms: ℒ A ​ ( T ) = 1 N ​ m ​ d ​ ‖ Q b ​ ( A ​ T ) − A ​ T ‖ F 2 , ℒ W ​ ( T ) = 1 o ​ d ​ ‖ Q b ​ ( W ​ T − ⊤ ) − W ​ T − ⊤ ‖ F 2 . \mathcal{L}_{A}(T)=\frac{1}{Nmd}\left\|Q_{b}(AT)-AT\right\|_{F}^{2},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{W}(T)=\frac{1}{od}\left\|Q_{b}(WT^{-\top})-WT^{-\top}\right\|_{F}^{2}. (8) The total loss is ℒ ​ ( T ) = ℒ out ​ ( T ) + λ A ​ ℒ A ​ ( T ) + λ W ​ ℒ W ​ ( T ) . \mathcal{L}(T)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{out}}(T)+\lambda_{A}\,\mathcal{L}_{A}(T)+\lambda_{W}\,\mathcal{L}_{W}(T). (9) Automatic scaling of λ \lambda . The regularization weights λ A \lambda_{A} and λ W \lambda_{W} are set so that each auxiliary term matches the magnitude of ℒ out \mathcal{L}_{\text{out}} at initialization: λ A = ℒ out ​ ( T 0 ) ℒ A ​ ( T 0 ) , λ W = ℒ out ​ ( T 0 ) ℒ W ​ ( T 0 ) , \lambda_{A}=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\text{out}}(T_{0})}{\mathcal{L}_{A}(T_{0})},\qquad\lambda_{W}=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\text{out}}(T_{0})}{\mathcal{L}_{W}(T_{0})}, (10) where T 0 T_{0} is the Hadamard initialization. This normalization ensures that none of the three terms dominates early in training, preventing the regularizers from overriding the primary output-error signal during the initial phase of optimization, while still providing sufficient gradient signal to avoid degenerate solutions. Optimization. We optimize ℒ ​ ( T ) \mathcal{L}(T) with respect to the 15 ⋅ ⌈ d / n ⌉ 15\cdot\lceil d/n\rceil free parameters of T T using Adam. The quantizer Q b Q_{b} is non-differentiable; we use a straight-through estimator (STE) to propagate gradients through the quantization operations. Since the transforms of the different layers are independent, they can be optimized in parallel or sequentially with negligible overhead relative to the calibration forward passes. The use of an STE and the Kronecker composition of the optimizable parameters makes the optimization unstable at a block or model level which is the reason why we keep the optimization at a layer level. 3.4 Final correction: offline LoRaQ weight calibration After optimizing the per-layer Kronecker transforms { T ( ℓ ) } \{T^{(\ell)}\} to minimize our objective, we apply the offline weight calibration procedure from LoRaQ (Bouquet et al. , 2026 ) to the transformed weights W ~ ( ℓ ) = W ( ℓ ) ​ ( T ( ℓ ) ) − ⊤ \widetilde{W}^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}(T^{(\ell)})^{-\top} . Bouquet et al. ( 2026 ) decomposes each transformed weight W ~ ( ℓ ) \widetilde{W}^{(\ell)} into a b b -bit quantized residual branch and an additive low-rank correction branch L ( ℓ ) ​ R ( ℓ ) L^{(\ell)}R^{(\ell)} , with L ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ o × r L^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{o\times r} and R ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ r × d R^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , and optimizes both branches data-free to carry most information of the 16-bit activation to the low-rank branch, reducing the linear layer’s overall quantization error further. The low-rank branch can itself be quantized below 16 bits without breaking the decomposition. At inference, the layer evaluates the quantized residual matrix multiplication and the mixed-precision low-rank correction in parallel and sums their outputs. Both kernels tile the activation matrix A ∈ ℝ m × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} on a 2D grid of shape ( ⌈ m / B R ⌉ , d / 32 ) (\lceil m/B_{R}\rceil,\;d/32) , where B R ∈ { 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } B_{R}\in\{16,32,64,128\} is autotuned. Each thread block processes a tile of shape ( B R , 32 ) (B_{R},32) . 3.5.1 Kernel variants K1 (precomputed dense). Each 32 × 32 32\times 32 block K ( j ) K^{(j)} is materialized and stored in HBM. The kernel loads the activation tile A tile ∈ ℝ B R × 32 A_{\text{tile}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B_{R}\times 32} and the corresponding K ( j ) ∈ ℝ 32 × 32 K^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times 32} , computes a single tl.dot( A tile A_{\text{tile}} , K block K_{\text{block}} ) accumulating in fp32, and stores the result after casting to the input dtype. Storage cost: 1024 values (2 KB) per column block; 256 KB total for d = 4096 d=4096 . K2 (on-the-fly Kronecker construction). Instead of loading a dense matrix, K2 reconstructs K ( j ) K^{(j)} from the 15 scalar parameters of the five 2 × 2 2\times 2 factors G 1 , … , G 5 G_{1},\ldots,G_{5} (Section 3.2 ). Since 32 = 2 5 32=2^{5} , every row and column index of K ( j ) K^{(j)} is a 5 5 -bit integer, and the Kronecker product entry-wise formula reads K ​ [ r , c ] = ∏ k = 1 5 G k ​ [ r 5 − k , c 5 − k ] , K[r,c]=\prod_{k=1}^{5}G_{k}\!\bigl[r_{5-k},\,c_{5-k}\bigr], (12) where r p r_{p} and c p c_{p} denote the p p -th bit of r r and c c respectively. The kernel applies this formula as a streaming product over the five factors, materializing K K factor-by-factor in registers via bit-indexed scalar lookups, leaving the register budget to fuse the downstream MXFP4e2 quantizer in the same kernel. Pseudocode is in Appendix B . Storage cost: 15 scalar parameters per column block, a ≈ 68 × \approx 68\times compression over K1. Both kernels satisfy the Triton tl.dot constraint M , N , K ≥ 16 M,N,K\geq 16 for all B R ≥ 16 B_{R}\geq 16 , since the GEMM shape is ( B R , 32 ) × ( 32 , 32 ) → ( B R , 32 ) (B_{R},32)\times(32,32)\to(B_{R},32) . K2 stores 15 scalar parameters per block ( 68 × 68\times compression over K1’s 1024 values) at a throughput cost of only 5–15% relative to K1 (see Appendix A ). For models with large hidden dimensions where many column blocks share the same Kronecker factors, K2’s parameter compression reduces HBM pressure on the transform-matrix read path. We evaluate on three diffusion transformers of increasing scale and architectural diversity: • PixArt- Σ \Sigma (Chen et al. , 2024a ) with 0.6 billion parameters, a single-stream architecture for text-to-image generation. • SANA (Xie et al. , 2025 ) with 1.6 billion parameters, a single-stream architecture for text-to-image generation with 1x1 convolution layers in the FFN module. • FLUX.1-schnell (Black-Forest-Labs, 2024 ) with 12 billion parameters, a double-stream architecture for text-to-image generation. Calibration dataset. Following the protocol of SVDQuant (Li et al. , 2025 ) and LoRaQ (Bouquet et al. , 2026 ) , we use 128 text prompts drawn from the COCO 2017 validation captions (Chen et al. , 2015 ) as calibration inputs. For each prompt a single forward pass is executed per linear layer to collect activation statistics used in transform optimization and LoRaQ weight calibration. Evaluation datasets. We report image quality on two different datasets, MJHQ-30K (Li et al. , 2024 ) and SDCI (Urbanek et al. , 2024 ) , each with 5,000 images randomly sampled with the same fixed-seed protocol following the evaluation split used in prior work. Metrics. Following existing benchmarks, we evaluate performance on two criteria. To measure similarity to the 16-bit baseline, we use Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (Zhang et al. , 2018 ) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR). To assess overall visual quality, we use Frechet Inception Distance (FID) (Heusel et al. , 2018 ) , Image Reward (IR) (Xu et al. , 2023 ) . Data format. We use MXFP4 E2M1 format following the OCP Microscaling (MX) standard (Microsoft et al. , 2023 ) , which is motivated by the fact that current hardware and software stacks, including Advanced Micro Devices ( 2025 ) and emerging ML frameworks, natively support MX formats at this granularity, as also adopted by Bouquet et al. ( 2026 ) . We refer to Appendix D for a description of the blockwise quantizer. We provide a full description of the experiments for reproducibility in Appendix D . 4.2 Main quantitative results Table 1 compares KroQuant against prior PTQ methods on PixArt- Σ \Sigma , SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell across two benchmarks. The smoothing method used by SVDQuant and LoRaQ are the same as described in Li et al. ( 2025 ); Bouquet et al. ( 2026 ) . KroQuant matches or improves upon all baselines on PixArt- Σ \Sigma and SANA across both benchmarks. On MJHQ-30K, KroQuant reduces LPIPS by 0.034 0.034 (relative 8.9 % 8.9\% ) over LoRaQ on PixArt- Σ \Sigma and by 0.023 0.023 ( 10.0 % 10.0\% ) on SANA, while closing the FID gap to the full-precision reference (16.9 vs. 16.6 on PixArt- Σ \Sigma ; matching 16.6 on SANA). The SDCI benchmark confirms these trends: KroQuant achieves the best FID, LPIPS, and PSNR on all three models, with particularly large LPIPS gains on FLUX.1-schnell ( 0.283 0.283 vs. 0.343 0.343 for LoRaQ, a 17.5 % 17.5\% relative reduction). On FLUX.1-schnell / MJHQ-30K, the picture is mixed: KroQuant achieves the best FID and PSNR but fails to improve over SVDQuant on IR and LoRaQ on LPIPS. We attribute this to the double-stream architecture of FLUX.1, where joint-attention blocks interleave text and image tokens with different activation distributions; a single per-layer Kronecker transform may underfit this heterogeneity. The consistent SDCI gains on FLUX.1 suggest the deficit is benchmark-dependent rather than systematic. Visual Results. This figure shows that KroQuant produces sharper images with fewer artifacts than the baselines, consistent with the improved quantitative metrics. Setup. All kernels run on an AMD Instinct MI350 in FP16, fuse a block-wise MXFP4e2 quantizer at their output, and are timed as medians over 500 repetitions after 100 warmup calls; reported latencies therefore reflect the full per-layer quantizer rather than the bare transform. At larger d d the fused Q4 quantizer dominates kernel time, leaving little headroom between any transform variant and the bare quantizer. 5 Conclusion and Limitations We presented KroQuant, a post-training quantization method for diffusion transformers that introduces learned Kronecker-structured block transforms as an online activation preprocessing step. The key observation is that AdaLN prevents the offline weight-absorption used by LLM rotation methods, and that a full-dimensional online transform is too costly. A block-diagonal learned transform parameterized via Kronecker products of 2 × 2 2\times 2 factors fills this gap at O ​ ( d ) O(d) parameter cost and tensor-core-native compute cost. The ablation confirms that the learned Kronecker transform provides strictly more expressive power than a fixed Hadamard initialization: starting from Hadamard (which matches per-channel smoothing on FID), gradient-based optimization of 15 parameters per block reduces LPIPS by 0.035 and improves PSNR by 0.8 dB on PixArt- Σ \Sigma . The hardware analysis shows that the transform’s block-diagonal structure keeps it single-pass and memory-bound, achieving near-bandwidth-optimal execution at 1.4 1.4 – 1.9 × 1.9\times the throughput of FWHT. KroQuant is complementary to weight-side corrections: the pipeline applies LoRaQ offline after the activation transforms are fixed, and the combination outperforms either component alone. On all three evaluated DiT architectures (PixArt- Σ \Sigma , SANA, FLUX.1-schnell), KroQuant achieves the best or competitive LPIPS and PSNR at MXFP4 E2M1 W4A4. Limitations. The Kronecker construction has only 3 ​ log 2 ⁡ n 3\log_{2}n parameters per n × n n\times n block, growing too slowly with block size to capture the full expressivity of GL ​ ( n ) \mathrm{GL}(n) at larger blocks; KroQuant therefore remains tied to n = 32 n=32 in practice. Joint multi-layer optimization is unstable in our experiments, partly due to the unit-determinant LU parametrization, leaving other parametrizations as future work. Finally, KroQuant outputs tend to have higher contrast than the FP16 reference, an empirical effect whose theoretical interpretation lies beyond the scope of this paper. Broader impacts.
